entities.name: Charles Ferdinand of Königsegg-Erps
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Count Karl Ferdinand von Königsegg-Erps (1696–1759) emerged as a pivotal figure in 18th-century Habsburg diplomacy and administration, serving as Imperial Vice-Chancellor and a key negotiator during the tumultuous War of the Austrian Succession. His career underscored the intricate balance of power politics and dynastic succession that defined the Early Modern European landscape, positioning him as a central architect of Austrian foreign policy under Empress Maria Theresa and an influential voice in the Holy Roman Empire's chancery.

Königsegg-Erps's diplomatic prowess was notably demonstrated in his role as the principal Habsburg plenipotentiary at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748, where he negotiated the treaty that formally concluded the War of the Austrian Succession, albeit with significant territorial concessions for Austria, including Silesia to Prussia. Prior to this, he held significant administrative posts, including Governor of the Austrian Netherlands from 1743 to 1744, a period marked by French invasion and strategic realignment. His consistent rise through the imperial bureaucracy, from Imperial Aulic Councillor to Vice-Chancellor in 1753, reflects his skill in navigating the complex web of European courts and internal Habsburg politics.

His contributions helped stabilize the Habsburg Monarchy in the aftermath of a devastating war and laid groundwork for the subsequent Diplomatic Revolution, which saw Austria align with France. Königsegg-Erps was instrumental in the administrative reforms initiated by Maria Theresa, aiming to centralize power and improve governmental efficiency across her diverse dominions. His work in the Imperial Chancery ensured a degree of continuity and expertise in foreign relations during a period of profound geopolitical shift.

entities.name: Charles Ferdinand of Königsegg-Erps
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Count Charles Ferdinand of Königsegg-Erps (1696–1759) was a preeminent Habsburg statesman and diplomat whose career spanned the reigns of Emperor Charles VI and Empress Maria Theresa. Born into the influential Swabian noble house of Königsegg-Erps in Vienna, his lineage provided him access to the highest echelons of Imperial service. His diplomatic acumen and administrative skill were critical in navigating the complex geopolitical landscape of 18th-century Europe, particularly during the tumultuous War of the Austrian Succession, where he worked to secure alliances and maintain the integrity of the Habsburg dominions.

Königsegg-Erps embarked on a distinguished diplomatic career, serving as Imperial envoy to the Electorate of Cologne before assuming the prestigious role of ambassador to the Court of France from 1725 to 1731. His subsequent appointment as ambassador to Spain (1731-1738) placed him at the heart of negotiations surrounding the War of the Polish Succession, culminating in the Treaty of Vienna (1738) which reshaped Italian territories. During the critical early years of the War of the Austrian Succession, he served as Imperial ambassador to the United Provinces (Dutch Republic) from 1740 to 1743, successfully lobbying for Dutch military and financial support for Maria Theresa against the Prussian and Franco-Bavarian coalition.

His administrative pinnacle came with his appointment as Governor-General of the Austrian Netherlands in 1743. Although his tenure was brief, concluding in 1744 due to the escalating war, he initiated efforts to stabilize the region amidst French incursions. Following this, he remained a key advisor in Vienna, contributing to strategic planning and the eventual Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748). His extensive network and experience provided continuity and expertise to the Habsburg foreign policy apparatus through a period of immense dynastic challenge, helping to preserve the monarchy's great power status.
